analyst:
Lehigh enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as the Patriot League’s automatic qualifier after winning the league tournament title game 74-60 over Boston University on March 11, 2026. That result moved the Mountain Hawks to 18-16 overall; before the Patriot League tournament they were 15-16 overall and 11-7 in league play, good for the No. 2 seed in the conference tournament. Official Lehigh game notes listed them at 10-15 overall and 6-6 in Patriot League play as of February 7, then 14-16 and 10-7 after the February 25 win at American, which tracks the late-season surge accurately. ([lehighsports.com](https://lehighsports.com/news/2026/3/12/mens-basketball-lehigh-wins-fourth-patriot-league-championship-in-74-60-victory-over-boston-university))

Offensively, this is a guard-led, inside-out team built around junior star Nasir Whitlock’s shot creation and sophomore big Hank Alvey’s interior efficiency. Whitlock led the Patriot League in scoring at 20.8 points per game entering postseason play, while Alvey averaged 14.6 points, 7.0 rebounds, and a league-best 1.8 blocks. Earlier official season stats had Whitlock at 19.9 points and 3.0 assists per game through February 7, with Alvey at 14.0 points on 62.6% shooting and 7.0 rebounds, showing the same offensive hierarchy all season. Lehigh’s offense repeatedly flows through high ball screens for Whitlock, duck-ins and seals for Alvey, and drive-and-kick actions that free Peter Kramer and Joshua Ingram for spot-up threes. A concrete example came in the February 25 win at American: Brett Reed specifically said Jalen Vazquez’s second-half point-guard work let Lehigh “move Nasir off the ball,” which created opportunities for Whitlock to score and for others to play through Alvey. In that same game, two Kramer threes capped a 10-1 run, and Lehigh scored 34 points in the paint. In the March 6 quarterfinal win over Holy Cross, Lehigh “attacked the paint early,” opening on an 8-0 run entirely on inside baskets, then toggled back to Whitlock pull-up shotmaking late. ([lehighsports.com](https://lehighsports.com/documents/download/2026/3/4/3-5_PL_QF_MBB_Game_Notes.pdf))

Specific play tendencies show up in their late-game offense. In the January 10 road win at Colgate, Alvey scored the game-winner on a layup with three seconds left after Lehigh had spent the day pairing Benoit floor spacing with Alvey rim pressure; Benoit finished with 27 points and 11 rebounds. In the January 31 overtime win over Colgate, Lehigh spread the floor for Whitlock isolation and pull-up creation; he scored 32 points and hit the game-winning jumper with 1.6 seconds left. In the February 22 win over Boston University, Lehigh erased a 13-point second-half deficit by leaning into downhill offense: a 10-0 run flipped the game, Whitlock hit a pull-up jumper with 8.9 seconds left, and Peter Kramer buried a corner three with under two minutes remaining. Those are not generic possessions; they show exactly what Lehigh trusts most: Whitlock in space, Alvey around the rim, and weak-side shooters ready on the catch. ([lehighsports.com](https://lehighsports.com/news/2026/1/10/mens-basketball-alveys-late-bucket-pushes-lehigh-past-colgate-78-77?utm_source=openai))

Defensively, Reed’s team plays with a traditional help-first philosophy: protect the lane, finish possessions with rebounding, and selectively pressure passing lanes rather than gambling constantly. The clearest evidence is in the title-game win over Boston University, when Lehigh held a team that entered shooting over 40% from three to 1-for-16 from deep, just 6.3%. In the March 6 quarterfinal against Holy Cross, Reed’s own postgame line was, “Defense wins,” after a final stop enabled Whitlock’s halfcourt winner. Against American on February 25, Lehigh limited the Eagles to 41.0% overall and 29.0% from three. When Lehigh loses, the defensive cracks are also specific: Army beat them 85-78 in overtime on December 31 while dominating the glass 46-26 and generating 17 second-chance points; Holy Cross beat them 76-67 on February 7 when Lehigh allowed 48.1% shooting and 82.6% at the foul line; Bucknell beat them 72-65 on January 3 after Reed said second-half turnovers gave up “run-out easy baskets.” The pattern is consistent: when Lehigh controls the boards and keeps the game in the half court, its defense is good enough to win. When it gets buried on the glass or gives away transition chances, it becomes vulnerable. ([lehighsports.com](https://lehighsports.com/news/2026/3/12/mens-basketball-lehigh-wins-fourth-patriot-league-championship-in-74-60-victory-over-boston-university))

Reed’s coaching philosophy is visible in documented in-game adjustments. Against American on February 25, he adjusted ball-handling responsibilities by using Vazquez more on the ball and Whitlock more off it in the second half; Reed said that shift “created opportunities” for Whitlock after a slow opening. Against Boston University on February 22, Lehigh trailed 22-14 in the first half and later by 13, but Reed’s group changed the game by shrinking the margin possession by possession, using Vaughquez/Whitlock penetration and Kramer’s spacing to trigger a comeback; the final sequence included a 10-0 run, a Whitlock pull-up, and disciplined foul-game execution. Against Holy Cross in the quarterfinal, Lehigh opened through paint touches, then survived a four-times-changed-hands second half by going back to Whitlock late and trusting Alvey’s hook game at 64-64. Reed’s teams have also shown willingness to live with overtime variance: Lehigh led the NCAA in overtime games played with seven entering the Patriot League quarterfinal, going 3-4 in those games at that point. ([lehighsports.com](https://lehighsports.com/news/2026/2/25/mens-basketball-lehigh-secures-quarterfinal-home-game-in-78-73-win-at-american))

Clutch execution is a real selling point. On January 14, Lehigh beat Boston University 93-91 in overtime after Whitlock banked in a game-tying three with 2.4 seconds left in regulation; Lehigh then went 12-for-12 from the foul line in overtime. On January 31, Whitlock scored 32 and hit the overtime winner with 1.6 seconds left in a 77-76 win over Colgate. On March 5, he beat Holy Cross 69-66 with a halfcourt buzzer-beater after first tying the game on a drive with 11.2 seconds left. On February 22, he hit a pull-up jumper with 8.9 seconds left to beat BU 70-67. Even in the January 8 win over Holy Cross, when the Crusaders cut the margin to four in the final minute, Whitlock made four clutch free throws and Nasir Whitlock/Edouard Benoit shot creation carried the closeout. The downside is that Lehigh also has evidence of late-game slippage: it lost 85-78 to Army in overtime after leading 67-63 with 1:40 left. ([lehighsports.com](https://lehighsports.com/news/2026/1/14/mens-basketball-lehigh-outlasts-boston-u-93-91-in-overtime-for-third-straight-win))

The key players are sharply defined. Whitlock is the alpha guard and late-clock closer. He scored a career-high 33 against Penn State Hazleton on December 18, led the league in scoring at 20.8 points per game entering the postseason, and was named Patriot League Championship MVP after the title run. His recent form was excellent: he earned Patriot League Player of the Week on March 2 after averaging 24.0 points and 5.5 assists in wins over American and Bucknell, and in the semifinal against Colgate he posted 22 points and a career-high 10 assists. Alvey is the interior finisher/rim protector. He averaged 14.6 points, 7.0 rebounds and 1.8 blocks, had three double-doubles entering the conference tournament, scored 24 points at American on February 25, and exploded for a career-high 30 in the March 8 semifinal against Colgate. Benoit is the secondary scoring forward who gives them rebound-and-shoot versatility; he had 27 points and 11 rebounds in the January 10 win at Colgate and 11 rebounds alone are tied to one of Lehigh’s best road performances. Kramer is the connective wing spacer; his corner three helped beat BU on February 22, and he hit three triples at American on February 25. Vazquez is the table-setter whose value shows up in Reed’s comments about moving Whitlock off the ball. ([lehighsports.com](https://lehighsports.com/documents/download/2026/3/4/3-5_PL_QF_MBB_Game_Notes.pdf))

Notable wins reveal what Lehigh can be at its ceiling. The March 11 title-game win over Boston University, 74-60, showed they can control a perimeter-heavy opponent by running shooters off the line and winning the glass 36-31. The March 8 semifinal win over Colgate, 76-69, showed frontcourt scoring power through Alvey’s 30 points and playmaking balance through Whitlock’s 22 points and 10 assists. The January 10 win at Colgate, 78-77, showed road resilience and two-man production from Benoit and Alvey. The February 25 win at American, 78-73, showed tactical flexibility and better two-way discipline against an upper-half Patriot League team. Notable losses reveal the weak points. The January 3 loss at Bucknell, 72-65, exposed turnover trouble and offensive over-penetration, in Reed’s words. The December 31 home loss to Army, 85-78 in overtime, exposed rebounding problems; Army’s 46-26 edge was overwhelming. The February 7 loss at Holy Cross, 76-67, showed how Lehigh’s offense can flatten when the three-point shot disappears; the Mountain Hawks shot only 3-for-20 from deep despite making 50.0% overall. ([lehighsports.com](https://lehighsports.com/news/2026/3/12/mens-basketball-lehigh-wins-fourth-patriot-league-championship-in-74-60-victory-over-boston-university))

As for head coach Brett Reed’s NCAA tournament history, Sports-Reference lists him with 2 NCAA Tournament appearances and a 1-2 tournament record before 2026. The most famous run came in 2012, when No. 15 seed Lehigh upset No. 2 Duke 75-70 in the Round of 64 before losing to Xavier in the next round; NCAA.com’s 2012 tournament archive confirms the Duke upset score. His other NCAA appearance was in 2010, when Lehigh lost in the first round. So Reed’s documented NCAA tournament history before this 2026 bid is: 2010, First Round loss; 2012, Round of 64 win over Duke and Round of 32 loss to Xavier. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/coaches/brett-reed-1.html?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: Lehigh is not built like a giant-killer that bombs 30 threes and plays chaos. This is a more traditional Reed team: one elite scoring guard in Whitlock, one highly efficient interior anchor in Alvey, secondary rebounding/scoring from Benoit, and a defense that can look tournament-viable when it owns the glass and forces opponents to beat it over bodies. The specific evidence from this season says the upset formula is clear: keep Whitlock in late-clock control situations, feed Alvey on seals and rolls, get enough spot shooting from Kramer/Ingram, and turn the game into a half-court possession battle the way Lehigh did against BU on March 11 and Colgate on March 8. ([lehighsports.com](https://lehighsports.com/news/2026/3/12/mens-basketball-lehigh-wins-fourth-patriot-league-championship-in-74-60-victory-over-boston-university))
forecaster:
Lehigh enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament profile as a low-major team with a respectable but clearly limited statistical résumé. Across the main public rating systems I could verify, the Mountain Hawks finished 16-16 overall and 11-7 in Patriot League play, with a NET of 275 on Warren Nolan’s team sheet, a predictive BPI of 288 on the NCAA-facing Warren Nolan aggregation, a KenPom/Pomeroy position of 284 on that same sheet, and a Torvik T-Rank of 283. ESPN’s Patriot League BPI page listed Lehigh at 245 as of its February 24, 2026 update, which suggests some model-to-model disagreement but still places them firmly in the lower third nationally. The broad takeaway is consistent: Lehigh was competitive within its conference, but national predictive systems viewed it as well below at-large caliber and outside the top 200 by a meaningful margin. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Lehigh))

On possession-based quality, Lehigh’s numbers point to a slightly below-average offense paired with a somewhat more fragile defense. Sports-Reference lists the Mountain Hawks at a 105.3 offensive rating and 107.0 defensive rating for the full season, while Warren Nolan’s Division I-only advanced stat pages show them at 108.1 points scored per 100 possessions and 109.1 allowed per 100. The exact figures differ by source because of methodology and opponent filtering, but the directional conclusion is the same: Lehigh was not disastrous on either side, yet it was underwater in net efficiency. Warren Nolan’s values imply roughly a -1.0 net rating; Sports-Reference’s season page similarly shows the team being outscored overall, 73.2 to 74.4 per game. That matters for tournament projection because teams in this tier generally need one bankable elite skill to survive a step up in class, and Lehigh’s profile is more “adequate across the board” than “dangerous in one defining way.” ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-offensive-rating?utm_source=openai))

Tempo is one of the clearest elements of the profile. Warren Nolan lists Lehigh’s pace at 64.7 possessions per 40 minutes, tied around 323rd nationally, so this is a slow team by modern standards. That slower pace has two implications. First, it can keep score margins from exploding against more talented opponents. Second, it compresses possessions enough that shooting variance matters more, which is relevant because Lehigh’s shot mix leans heavily into the three. Their three-point attempt rate was 0.494, sixth nationally on Warren Nolan, an unusually high-flyer profile for a team that otherwise plays slowly. That contrast is important analytically: Lehigh does not push pace, but once it is in the half court it is comfortable ending possessions with threes. Conventional wisdom may see a Patriot League team with a middling record and assume plodding, interior-first basketball; the data says Lehigh is actually a slow-but-bombing perimeter offense. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-pace?utm_source=openai))

The shooting and possession component stats reinforce that picture. Lehigh posted a 53.3% effective field goal percentage, good for roughly 94th nationally on Warren Nolan, and shot .465 from the field and .356 from three on Sports-Reference. Those are real positives. Free-throw shooting was acceptable rather than a major weapon: Sports-Reference has them at .732, while Warren Nolan’s offense page rounds them to 73.0%. Where the profile breaks down is on the glass and in possession volume. Lehigh’s offensive rebound percentage was only 22.2%, 354th nationally, one of the weakest marks in Division I. In plain terms, they rarely generated second chances. They also averaged about 12.3 to 12.5 turnovers per game depending on source, which is not catastrophic but is loose enough that a team without offensive-rebounding support can struggle to create enough shots. So the offensive identity is efficient first-shot shooting, especially via the jumper, but very little cleanup behind misses and only middling ball security. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-efg-percent?utm_source=openai))

Strength of schedule is another major anchor on the résumé. Sports-Reference lists Lehigh’s SOS at -6.79, 304th nationally, while Warren Nolan’s team sheet gives them a NET SOS of 319 and a non-conference SOS of 181. Their Division I non-conference record was just 2-9, and quadrant performance was thin: 0-2 in Q1, 0-1 in Q2, 1-5 in Q3, and 15-8 in Q4. That is the statistical skeleton of a team that handled a fair share of beatable opponents but did not produce quality wins against stronger competition. Even within the softer schedule context, Lehigh’s average NET of teams it beat was 283, while the average NET of teams it lost to was 210. In tournament translation, that means the raw shooting competence has to be interpreted carefully; it was built against a schedule that did not consistently stress-test it. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/lehigh/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Recent-form data is more limited in exact trendline form, but the available evidence suggests Lehigh was competitive late rather than surging into elite shape. ESPN’s team page had them 13-16 with a Patriot League tournament quarterfinal win six days before crawl time, and Sports-Reference captured the final full season at 17-16 including the conference tournament. There is no accessible public last-10 efficiency table from the major premium sources in the retrieved results, but their end-of-year arc appears closer to stabilized mid-league contender than to a team making a massive March leap. The strongest evidence is that their underlying season metrics remained in the high-200s nationally even after the full sample closed. That implies any late wins improved results more than they transformed the underlying power profile. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2329/lehigh-mountain-hawks/1000?utm_source=openai))

The eye-test/data split is probably this: Lehigh likely looks more dangerous on offense than its national ranking suggests because it has credible shot-making and real perimeter volume, led by Nasir Whitlock’s 21.1 points per game and supported by multiple double-figure scorers including Hank Alvey, Joshua Ingram, and Edouard Benoit. A viewer could come away thinking this is a live underdog because the spacing and shooting are functional. But the deeper metrics push back. The defense is only mediocre, the rebounding is poor, the schedule was weak, and the profile against top-three quadrants was almost empty. So the numbers say Lehigh is more aesthetically dangerous than substantively dangerous: a team capable of hanging around if the threes fall, but without the possession dominance, defensive resistance, or résumé proof that usually underpins a true bracket-busting threat. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/lehigh/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: Lehigh’s 2025-26 statistical profile is that of a slow-tempo, perimeter-leaning, moderately efficient offensive team with severe offensive-rebounding limitations, middling defensive quality, and a weak strength-of-schedule foundation. The best-case tournament case is obvious: low pace plus high three-point volume can create upset variance. The worst-case case is just as obvious: against high-major length and physicality, the lack of extra possessions and the ordinary defensive numbers leave almost no margin for error. The profile is coherent, but it is not deceptive. Lehigh was solid in its league, shoot-first in style, and nationally rated in the high-200 range by most predictive systems. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-pace?utm_source=openai))
matchup-analyst:
Lehigh enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a 16-seed at 18-16 overall after winning the Patriot League, but the underlying profile says this is an offense-led team with real shot-making and real structural weaknesses. Their team averages are 73.2 points, 46.4% FG, 35.9% from three, only 31.9 rebounds per game, and 12.1 turnovers per game; Bracketologists’ through-March-15 team sheet also had them 350th nationally in offensive rebounds at 7.68 per game and 327th in rebound margin at minus-4.0. The identity starts with junior guard Nasir Whitlock, who averages 21.0 points and 3.4 assists, and sophomore forward Hank Alvey, who averages 15.0 points, 6.9 rebounds, 1.8 blocks and shoots 62.4% from the field. Joshua Ingram adds 10.6 points, 5.1 rebounds and 3.3 assists. Shot distribution strongly suggests an isolation-tilted lead-guard offense layered over secondary ball movement: Whitlock alone used 496 field-goal attempts and 207 free-throw attempts in 34 games, while the entire team produced 487 assists on 886 made baskets, an assist rate of roughly 55.0%; Whitlock took 26.0% of all Lehigh field-goal attempts and scored 28.6% of its points, so the offense repeatedly flows back to one-on-one creation late in possessions. 

Style of play: Lehigh is most comfortable in a guard-driven half-court attack that hunts perimeter pull-ups and empty-side drives for Whitlock, then plays through Alvey as a power finisher. Whitlock made 77 threes at 44.5%, Ingram made 47 at 38.8%, Peter Kramer made 36 at 37.5%, and the team hit 35.9% from deep, so clean catch-and-shoot help is dangerous. The disruption formula is specific: top-lock Whitlock off pin-downs, switch or hard-show his ball screens, then crowd Alvey with a second body on the catch because Lehigh is not an elite offensive-rebounding team and does not punish aggressive help on the glass. The best evidence is their loss at Navy, 72-49 on February 18, when Lehigh scored a season-low 49; by contrast, when Whitlock gets downhill and the game opens, Lehigh has posted 90 against American on February 11, 89 against Bucknell on February 28, and 93 at Boston University on January 14. The tactical takeaway is that physical point-of-attack defense plus tempo control matters more than selling out to deny every touch. 

Press vulnerability: Lehigh is not catastrophically turnover-prone overall, but they are vulnerable when opponents turn live-ball pressure into long empty stretches. In the December 6 loss to LIU, Lehigh committed 19 turnovers and went more than six minutes without a field goal during the first-half collapse from 9-8 to 29-10; that is your cleanest named example of ball pressure knocking them out of rhythm. Their own game notes also show a binary result split: through the quarterfinal notes, Lehigh was 11-11 when committing fewer than 15 turnovers and only 4-5 when committing 15 or more. Against Marist on November 25, they lost 78-55 and never generated enough offensive continuity to recover after a poor start. So the pressing blueprint is not reckless 40-minute gambling; it is selective pressure after makes, token three-quarter-court heat, and loaded nail help on Whitlock to force the ball into secondary handlers like Vazquez, Thomas, or Urosevic.

Zone vulnerability: there is less direct public possession-tag data on how Lehigh performs specifically versus zone, so the safest evidence-based inference comes from game shape and personnel. Lehigh is dangerous against soft zone if Whitlock can pull up and if Alvey can occupy the middle, but they become more ordinary when forced into extra passes by compact help because only Whitlock is both high-volume and elite-efficiency from three. Benoit shot 30.8% from three, Urosevic 33.3%, Vazquez 28.9%, Thomas 18.8%, and Addesa 28.1%. That means a packed-in 2-3 or matchup zone can stunt Whitlock’s drives and dare weaker-volume spacers to beat you over time. The best game evidence is Navy’s 72-49 win and Houston’s 75-57 win on November 3: different defenses, same outcome—Lehigh struggled when drives were crowded and the game became a possession-by-possession shot-quality battle. Because Lehigh shot just 28.6% from three against LIU as well, an opponent can mix zone possessions after timeouts to cool their primary creators rather than playing it full time.

Preferred pace: Lehigh wants a moderate game where Whitlock can hunt early offense without turning it into a pure transition track meet. Their schedule is full of overtime and 70-plus-possession-feel games: 93-91 at Boston University, 82-79 2OT vs Navy, 89-84 2OT at Loyola Maryland, 90-82 vs American, 89-79 vs Bucknell. They are more comfortable when the score rises into the 70s and 80s. To force the opposite, you must shorten the game, make them defend deep into the clock, and eliminate live-ball turnovers that feed their rhythm threes. Again, Navy is the template: 72-49, Whitlock got 20, but the rest of the offense never got traction. Houston’s 75-57 season opener is the high-major version of the same script. 

Size and athleticism mismatches by position: at point/lead guard, Whitlock is 6-2, 184, productive but not oversized; a bigger 6-4 or 6-5 on-ball defender can bother his sightlines. At the secondary guard spots, Ingram is 6-4/176 and Kramer is 6-5/196, so Lehigh has decent wing length but not overwhelming burst. At the small-ball forward spots, Benoit is 6-8/207 and Pike is 6-8/210, while Alvey is a true load at 6-9/251. That means they can create a strength mismatch against lighter fours through Alvey, but they can also be exposed by explosive, switchable athletes who can front the post and beat them down the floor. At center, Henri Adiassa is 6-11/240 and Tommy Conniff is 6-11/260, but neither is a major offensive hub in the season stats; Lehigh’s scoring and usage remain perimeter-dominant. So the most likely mismatch against Lehigh is not pure height, but speed and lateral quickness at the 1-3 and rim-running athleticism versus their bigger frontcourt rotation.

Transition offense and defense: public sources here do not provide Synergy-style exact transition-possession frequency, so I cannot honestly give a precise national-percentile split. What the results do show is that Lehigh thrives when games become unstable and scoring swings happen quickly: they erased a 13-point second-half deficit to beat Boston University 70-67 on February 22, erased a 13-point second-half deficit earlier in the year to beat American 90-82, and rallied from multiple deficits in the Patriot tournament, including the 69-66 quarterfinal win over Holy Cross and the 74-60 title-game win over Boston University. On the other side, they are vulnerable in defensive transition or scramble phases when ball security slips; LIU’s 19 forced turnovers and Bucknell’s comeback from a 36-28 halftime deficit are examples of Lehigh failing to control game flow. The safest data-backed statement is that live-ball chaos helps their offense less than you might think because their turnover threshold is so important to winning.

Coaching adaptability: Brett Reed absolutely has evidence of in-game adjustment. Lehigh’s season is full of comeback wins and tactical recoveries rather than wire-to-wire dominance. They erased a 13-point second-half deficit to beat American 90-82, erased a 13-point second-half deficit to beat Boston University 70-67 on February 22, won the quarterfinal after Holy Cross repeatedly changed the lead in the second half, and then held Boston University to 1-for-16 from three in the Patriot title game after BU entered shooting above 40% from deep. That title-game defensive result is the clearest proof that Reed’s staff can change coverage emphasis and personnel usage on short turnaround prep. I would not call it “mid-series” adaptability in the NBA-playoff sense because college does not play series, but within a game and across consecutive tournament games, the evidence says yes.

Concrete gameplan: To beat this team you must do four things. First, put a long defender on Whitlock and show him two bodies at the nail; make Ingram, Vazquez, Thomas, and Benoit create off the bounce. Second, pressure selectively and target the 15-turnover line, because Lehigh was 4-5 when committing 15 or more turnovers and LIU’s 19 forced giveaways directly fueled an 87-82 road win. Third, own the glass with physicality because Lehigh was 350th nationally in offensive rebounds and minus-4.0 in rebound margin; if you finish possessions, their second-chance counters are limited. Fourth, keep the game ugly and slow. Navy’s 72-49 win and Houston’s 75-57 win are the best templates: crowd driving lanes, force contested jumpers from the non-Whitlock shooters, and make Lehigh score late in the clock rather than in rhythm. If you let Whitlock get comfortable early and let Alvey catch deep without second-side pressure, Lehigh can absolutely play above seed line. But if you win the turnover battle, rebound, and force half-court execution from their secondary creators, the matchup tilts sharply against them.
